The first payment goes to your municipality. After the local deadline, the Kenosha County Treasurer takes over. The office is at 1010 56th Street, Kenosha, WI 53140, phone 262-653-2542. It administers the property tax laws, collects delinquent tax and settles each year with the county's municipalities, school districts, Gateway Technical College and the Wisconsin Department of Revenue.

Second and later installments, and delinquent tax, can be paid in person at the downtown office on 56th Street (8 am to 5 pm, Monday through Friday) or at the Elected Officials Office in the Kenosha County Center, where Highways 45 and 50 meet in Bristol (8 am to 4:30 pm, Monday through Friday). Under Wis. Stat. 74.11(6), payments made on or before January 31 go to the municipal treasurer, and all other payments go to the county treasurer unless your bill says otherwise.

The county's Property & Taxes page links to a Property Inquiry portal showing tax bills, assessments, sales and building data for a parcel, plus current and past county mill rates.

The full amount or first installment is due on or before January 31. Where the second installment goes depends on the municipality.

Where the parcel isInstallmentsPay to
City of KenoshaFull payment, or three installments due Jan 31, Apr 30 and Jul 31City of Kenosha through July 31
Village of Pleasant PrairieFull payment, or three installments due Jan 31, Apr 30 and Jul 31Village of Pleasant Prairie through July 31
All other municipalitiesFull payment or first installment by Jan 31Local town or village treasurer for Jan 31; Kenosha County Treasurer for the second installment and anything delinquent

Bills are mailed in mid-December, and state law (74.09(5)) sets the mailing deadline at the third Monday in December. If nothing has arrived by about December 20, call your municipal treasurer, because under 74.09(6) a missing bill does not excuse a late payment.

The first-installment date of January 31, 2027 falls on a Sunday. When January 31 lands on a weekend, the five-working-day window runs through the first Friday in February (74.11(7)(b) and 74.12(7)(b)), which is February 5, 2027. Confirm the exact cutoff with your treasurer before relying on it.

The whole unpaid balance becomes delinquent and the installment option ends. If the first installment is missed, the entire remaining tax is delinquent as of February 1 (74.11(7) and 74.12(7)). If the July 31 installment is missed, the unpaid balance is delinquent as of August 1, and interest and penalty are charged back to February 1.

Interest is 1 percent per month under 74.47(1), with part of a month counted as a whole one, plus a 0.5 percent monthly penalty that a county can add by ordinance under 74.47(2). Kenosha County lists the combined charge as 18 percent a year. State law sets these amounts, and the treasurer's office cannot adjust them.

Prior-year delinquent tax is always paid at the County Treasurer's Office. The county will set up a payment plan on these terms:

  • Prior-year taxes must be paid within 10 months for each delinquent year, so one year gets 10 months and two years get 20.
  • Three years in delinquent status starts the tax deed foreclosure process, and the property can be lost.
  • Current-year installments must also be paid on time during the plan.
  • Missing a plan payment, or letting current-year tax go delinquent, cancels the plan and makes the whole balance due. Two missed plan payments cancel it.

Owners in the City of Kenosha or Pleasant Prairie who fall behind on current-year tax should call their local treasurer before July 31 and the County Treasurer after that date.

Several methods work, and a few details matter for mail and online payments.

  • Mail: send your payment with the stub from the top of the bill. If you want a receipt, enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope. Near a deadline, take the envelope to the post office and ask for a hand postmark. A bank's bill-pay check often has no postmark, and the bank's confirmation does not prove timely payment.
  • In person: cash, check, money order or cashier's check at either county office. Credit cards are also accepted.
  • Online: through the Property Inquiry portal with the 13-digit parcel identification number from your bill. Credit card transactions carry a fee, and electronic check is also offered.
  • Phone: 1-888-891-6064, extension 2.

Under 74.69(1), a payment is timely if it is in a properly addressed envelope, postmarked on or before the due date with postage prepaid, and received within five working days after the due date. Owners with a mortgage escrow remain responsible for the tax. Check that the lender really paid it, and think twice before asking that all notices go to the mortgage company.

The municipality where the property sits sets the assessment, so the appeal starts there. Each municipality's Board of Review meets once a year during the 45-day window that begins on the fourth Monday in April, and no sooner than 7 days after the assessment roll closes for examination (70.47(1)). The clerk must publish notice at least 15 days before the first session, or 30 days before in a revaluation year (70.47(2)).

To be heard, give the board clerk written or oral notice of intent to object at least 48 hours before the first meeting. Then file the written objection within the first two hours of that meeting (70.47(7)(a)). An owner of land and improvements can object only to the combined value. If you disagree with the board's decision, the next step is an action for certiorari in court, which must start within 90 days after you receive the board's notice (70.47(13)).

To prepare for next year, ask your municipal assessor when open book is scheduled and which clerk handles Board of Review filings.

The Wisconsin Lottery and Gaming Credit goes to owners whose home was their primary residence on January 1. The county's Property & Taxes page has a Lottery Credit search so you can confirm you receive it, and the county treasurer or your municipal treasurer can send an application. A lottery credit stays with the property until the owner or the Department of Revenue removes it, and a late claim after the first installment date needs a copy of your latest tax bill uploaded before October 1.

Lower-income owners can look at the Homestead Credit, filed with state income taxes. Disabled service members and surviving spouses may qualify for a separate state property tax credit through the County service office. The treasurer cannot forgive interest for hardship.

The purchase contract usually divides the sale year's taxes between seller and buyer. If the contract is silent, Wis. Stat. 74.15 makes the seller pay the buyer one-twelfth of the prior year's taxes for each month elapsed before the conveyance, counting the sale month when the deed date falls after the 15th. The municipal treasurer accepts taxes paid ahead of the levy from August 1 until the third Monday in December (74.13), so a seller who wants the year settled can prepay.

If the parcel is delinquent, the payoff comes from the County Treasurer and includes interest and penalty through the closing date. Ask the treasurer's office at 262-653-2542 for a written figure good through the day you expect to close. Special assessments and special charges on the bill are collected like the tax, and a missed special charge can make the whole parcel delinquent (74.11(10)(b)).

A cash buyer does not change any of this. The tax payoff still comes out of the proceeds, though without a lender the timeline is usually shorter.

Kenosha County is in the southeast corner of Wisconsin on the western shore of Lake Michigan, with Racine County to the north and Walworth County to the west. Metra's Union Pacific North Line links it to Chicago. Population is 168,448, the eighth highest among Wisconsin counties. The median owner-occupied home is worth $265,500, 66.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied, median household income is $81,239 and median gross rent is $1,219. Besides the City of Kenosha, the county includes villages such as Pleasant Prairie, Bristol, Paddock Lake, Salem Lakes and Twin Lakes, and towns such as Brighton, Paris, Randall and Wheatland.

faqs.q: When are Kenosha County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The full amount or first installment is due by January 31. Second installments go to the County Treasurer after that, except in the City of Kenosha and Village of Pleasant Prairie, which collect three installments (Jan 31, Apr 30, Jul 31) and keep current-year payments through July 31.

faqs.q: What interest does Kenosha County charge on late property tax?
faqs.a: Delinquent tax carries 1 percent interest per month under Wis. Stat. 74.47(1) plus a 0.5 percent monthly penalty, which the county lists as 18 percent a year. The charge runs back to February 1 and the treasurer cannot waive it.

faqs.q: Can I get a payment plan for delinquent Kenosha County taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The County Treasurer sets up plans for prior-year taxes, requiring payment within 10 months for each delinquent year and on-time current-year installments. Three years of delinquency starts tax deed foreclosure.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Kenosha County property tax online?
faqs.a: Use the Property Inquiry portal linked from the county's Property & Taxes page. You need the 13-digit parcel number from your bill, and credit card payments carry a fee. For City of Kenosha parcels, current-year payments through July 31 go to the city, not the county.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Kenosha County assessment?
faqs.a: Contact your municipal assessor first, then file with the municipal Board of Review. Give notice of intent at least 48 hours before the first meeting and file the written objection in the first two hours (Wis. Stat. 70.47(7)(a)). Court review by certiorari must start within 90 days of the board's notice.
